place-work.text: Molded clay, practical household production and public gathering places reveal related kinds of work. Their interpretation depends on a particular room, sample, source and community relationship; neither one revised date nor one later council building supplies an unchanged institution for all people and periods.

interval.label: Earthlodge construction chronology under revision
interval.note: No settled construction/use endpoints are plotted. The older 1015 label is a median of early radiocarbon determinations; newer roof-wood evidence indicates cutting sometime after c.1160 and leaves possible earlier construction unresolved. Neither observation dates the lifespan of Muscogee people or the whole Ocmulgee site.

New roof-wood evidence indicates cutting sometime after c.1160; possible earlier construction remains unresolved.

question: How can a building bring people together while its history remains open to revision?
summary: People shaped clay, raised supports, stored food and made places for gathering at Ocmulgee. Surviving features, retained samples and current Muscogee perspectives make different parts of that history visible. A revised timber date changes the inquiry without replacing the building’s disputed case with an invented construction span.

sections.title: Making a room for gathering
sections.text: Building the Earthlodge joined several materials and tasks. People shaped clay into a floor, seats and a bird-shaped platform, while timber supported the roof. Its circular form differed from the smaller rectangular homes described in the park bulletin. A central hearth and arranged places to sit brought people into a shared space. The published feature drawing also records fallen roof posts: excavation preserves a building’s changes, rather than displaying every part as it originally stood.

sections.title: Food and containers supported other work
sections.text: Daily production helped sustain life around the public buildings. The NPS account describes Macon Plateau farmers cultivating with wood, bone and stone tools, storing food in baskets and pottery, and forming pots from local clay. These activities turned plants and materials into supplies that could be kept and used. They extend the explanation beyond monumental building, while remaining a park synthesis rather than an inventory of one family’s meals or a roster of the Earthlodge’s builders.

sections.title: Different gathering places suggest different relationships
sections.text: Archaeologists identified more than one large public building at Ocmulgee. The collaborative study compares the Earthlodge with Council Chamber 2 and considers whether overlapping use could support smaller groups within the wider settlement. Meeting, debating and maintaining shared places could involve several communities. That remains an interpretation, not proof that one chief directed every task, that every lodge had the same function or that the occupants of each seat can be named.

sections.title: Retained material makes new questions possible
sections.text: Researchers returned to wood and cane retained from the earlier excavations. Their analysis places cutting of a selected roof timber after about 1160, while other evidence leaves an earlier structure possible. The familiar 1015 label comes from older radiocarbon work. Those observations answer different questions. The clay floor survives beneath walls and ceiling reconstructed in the late 1930s; neither the exterior photograph nor a laboratory estimate supplies the day a complete room was finished.

sections.title: Living relationships shape research
sections.text: In Braden Harper’s 2026 report, RaeLynn Butler explains collaboration through mutual benefit and the value of Muscogee knowledge. Turner Hunt describes an opportunity to reframe histories that excluded Native voices. Their attributed perspectives help explain why the questions matter now. The Muscogee Nation’s Council House museum in Okmulgee presents a separate history of government, forced displacement and recovery. It is a later Oklahoma institution, connected through people and memory, rather than the same building transported from Georgia.

deeperReading.title: A timber constraint is not a building birthday
deeperReading.text: A tree grows before anyone cuts or uses it. The new Earthlodge analysis compares retained growth rings and radiocarbon measurements to constrain the timber’s history. The authors describe cutting sometime after about 1160, not a precisely observed construction event. An earlier cane sample and a reported burned layer leave earlier building work possible. Retaining the original disputed interval allows the different materials and interpretations to remain open to review.

deeperReading.title: A feature plan can record change
deeperReading.text: The source drawing distinguishes bench seats, internal supports, hearth and entrance from fallen roof material. Read its labels as an interpreted excavation record. The modern exterior shelter protects ancient clay, but its roof cannot be used as an untouched ancient model. The NPS bulletin also questions an earlier inference that seat size mapped social rank. A visible difference can prompt a question without recovering its social meaning or the words spoken in the room.

deeperReading.title: Continuity does not require an unchanged settlement
deeperReading.text: The Middle Plateau dates challenge a simple occupation gap, but the study cannot yet distinguish a larger settlement from a few farmsteads throughout that period. A laboratory model is therefore not a census. The Council House’s own history follows a distinct later institution through governmental use, dispossession and regained control. Butler’s and Hunt’s current statements add their own priorities; they are not reconstructed ancient speeches or evidence that every descendant community endorses one account.

evidenceReading.title: Surviving clay, dated wood and attributed voices
evidenceReading.introduction: These passages paraphrase the consulted sources. A photograph, an archaeological drawing, a laboratory model and present-day statements support different explanations.

items.label: The floor and the shelter have different histories
items.text: NPS identifies the clay floor as surviving material and the walls and ceiling as a late-1930s reconstruction. Its feature record includes arranged seats, a hearth and a raised bird-shaped platform.
items.interpretation: The interior photograph supplies a visible clay-and-timber comparison; the source drawing adds feature relationships. Neither supplies an unchanged ancient roof, a roll call or a recovered discussion. The exterior is a modern protective building.

items.label: The new date concerns a selected sample
items.text: The study places cutting of selected roof wood after about 1160 and retains a possible earlier building. It explains the old 1015 label as a median from earlier radiocarbon work.
items.interpretation: A material date constrains a construction explanation without fixing its exact beginning or end. Other samples and assumptions matter; the original disputed case must not become a span drawn between unlike dates.

items.label: Current participants explain the value of collaboration
items.text: Harper attributes to Butler a model of research in which participants benefit and Muscogee knowledge matters; Hunt describes reframing narratives that previously excluded Native voices.
items.interpretation: These are named contemporary perspectives reported by Mvskoke Media. Attribute them rather than turning them into an ancient belief, a universal position or approval of this atlas. No article photograph or protected knowledge is reproduced.

familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: NPS distinguishes surviving archaeological clay from walls and roof reconstructed in the late 1930s. The older 1015 label is disputed by a collaborative study of retained samples. Selected roof wood was cut after about 1160, while an earlier structure remains possible. The photograph can show material and position; it cannot by itself supply the roof’s construction year, a list of participants or a conversation. Current Muscogee relationships are represented through attributed sources, not invented speeches.

review.reviewer: Codex selected primary/institutional consultation and internal author review; not independent historian or community approval
review.scope: Selected practical building and household work, three evidence readings, a supplied two-photograph family activity, separately qualified reference phases and an inspected published feature drawing. The entire original disputed interval, both alternatives/citations, identity, claims, old object order, dimensions and image bytes remain intact. A sample date and a research frame do not replace the unresolved building chronology.
limitations: No settled Earthlodge construction/use span supplied. The old 1015 median, later roof-timber constraint, possible earlier structure and distinct area/sample models must not be combined into an invented exact interval.

The current NPS place page, gallery and bulletin still retain older date language. Practical-work passages do not establish a population count, universal gendered division of labor, necessary centralized chief or identical function for every structure.

Selected publisher HTML and Figure 3 pixels were consulted; not the entire printed volume, every table/figure, original Fairbanks/WPA records, raw sample or supplementary model file. No independent calibration rerun. Council Chamber 2 and Middle Plateau estimates remain separate from the selected room.

Figure 3 has an internal caption/panel mismatch. The inspected bird-platform drawing is used only as the qualified D-1 feature record, not a Council Chamber 2 plan. Its excavation-state fallen roof material is not a standing-roof reconstruction; no new survey or unrecorded plan crop is claimed.

Both existing photographs retain their original bytes and unknown exposure dates. The small 526×339 interior scan gains no newly recovered detail. The included source composite has article-specific CC BY 4.0 and full source/adaptation credit; its modern creation/exposure dates are not supplied by publication dates.

Butler and Hunt are named contemporary perspectives; the Council House is a distinct later Oklahoma institution. Neither collaboration nor an archaeological model supplies universal descendant assent, an unchanged institution, a geographic route or recovered ancient speech.
Independent historian/community review, real family use, human screen-reader behavior, physical-device testing and physical print quality remain open.
